title: Revision HQ 2: lessons 9 to 13
starter: Without notes, list as many key terms from lessons 9 to 13 as you can in two minutes.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Lesson 9: Modes of connection
facts: Ethernet is wired: fast, reliable and secure, but needs cabling.
Wi-Fi is wireless, about 100 m range, high bandwidth.
Bluetooth: about 10 m, low bandwidth, low power.
stations.challenge: Which is better: a wired or wireless network?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Ethernet is wired: fast, reliable and secure, but needs cabling.
Also credit: Wi-Fi is wireless, about 100 m range, high bandwidth.

questions.q: Which connection has a range of about 10 metres and low power use?
Which is an advantage of a wired connection?
questions.a: More reliable and easier to secure

questions.q: What does Ethernet send data in?
questions.a: Frames with source and destination addresses

stations.name: Lesson 10: Wi-Fi encryption
facts: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it.
A public key is shared; a private key is never shared.
WPA2 authenticates devices without sending the key.
stations.challenge: What is the purpose of encryption?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it.
Also credit: A public key is shared; a private key is never shared.

questions.q: Why is encryption needed on Wi-Fi?
questions.a: Signals can be intercepted by anyone in range

questions.q: Which key must never be shared?
What does WPA2 do before data is sent?
questions.a: Authenticates the devices using keys made from the password

stations.name: Lesson 11: IP and MAC addressing
facts: MAC: 48 bits, hexadecimal pairs, set when the NIC is made; used in a LAN.
IPv6: 128 bits, hexadecimal groups; needed because IPv4 ran out.
stations.challenge: What are the differences between the three types of address?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: MAC: 48 bits, hexadecimal pairs, set when the NIC is made; used in a LAN.
Also credit: IPv4: 32 bits, four numbers 0 to 255.

questions.q: Which address does a switch use?

stations.name: Lesson 12: Standards and protocols
facts: Standards let hardware and software from different makers work together.
A protocol is a set of rules for communication.
HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP, IMAP, TCP/IP.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Standards let hardware and software from different makers work together.
Also credit: A protocol is a set of rules for communication.

questions.q: Which protocol sends email to a mail server?
What does HTTPS add to HTTP?

questions.a: Makes sure packets arrive without errors and in order

stations.name: Lesson 13: Layers
facts: Networking is divided into layers, each with a defined job.
Each layer provides a service to the layer above.
A layer can be changed without affecting the others.
stations.challenge: What are the benefits of layering protocols?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Networking is divided into layers, each with a defined job.
Also credit: Each layer provides a service to the layer above.

questions.a: To divide a complex task into smaller, simpler tasks

questions.q: Which is an advantage of layering?
questions.a: One layer can be changed without affecting the others

questions.q: Which layer does Wi-Fi belong to?

stations.name: Exam technique
facts: State: give a short fact. Describe: give the key features. Explain: say how or why, using 'because'.
Match your answer to the marks: one point per mark.
Use the key terms from this unit.
stations.challenge: Which command word needs you to give a reason?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: State: give a short fact. Describe: give the key features. Explain: say how or why, using 'because'.
Also credit: Match your answer to the marks: one point per mark.

questions.q: A question says 'Explain'. What do you need to include?
questions.a: Reasons: how or why something happens

questions.q: How many points should you aim for in a 4-mark question?
A question says 'State'. What is expected?

final.name: Final challenge: key terms

questions.q: Match each key term to its meaning.
questions.a: Ethernet → A wired standard for connecting devices on a LAN; Bluetooth → Short-range, low-power wireless connection between two devices; Encryption → Scrambling data so it can't be read without the key; IPv6 → A 128-bit address, written in hexadecimal; Protocol → A set of rules for how devices communicate; Layer → A part of networking with one defined responsibility

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Explain one advantage of using IPv6 instead of IPv4.
points: IPv6: 128 bits, hexadecimal groups; needed because IPv4 ran out.
State: give a short fact. Describe: give the key features. Explain: say how or why, using 'because'.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Describe how public and private keys are used.
points: A public key is shared; a private key is never shared.
MAC: 48 bits, hexadecimal pairs, set when the NIC is made; used in a LAN.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
